ethiopia.content: Ethiopia Advances African Leadership, National Development and Strategic Interests - ENA English - ENA Skip to Content Ethiopia Advances African Leadership, National Development and Strategic Interests - ENA English Live: አማርኛ ትግርኛ Afaan Oromoo Af‑Soomaali Qafar Afa English Français عربي Politics Social Economy Sport Technology Environment Feature Videos About Us Ethiopia Advances African Leadership, National Development and Strategic Interests 🔇Unmute By Staff Writer October 25, 2026 (ENA) Ethiopia’s key developments this week highlighted an interconnected national agenda: strengthening African leadership, accelerating economic transformation, building institutional capacity and safeguarding strategic interests amid a rapidly changing regional and global order. From the 12th Tana High-Level Forum on Security in Africa to the inauguration of the Megech Dam, the country’s engagements reflected a broader effort to connect continental cooperation with tangible development outcomes at home. Economic reforms, agricultural modernization, technological capacity-building and the National Dialogue further underscored the importance of building a resilient state capable of translating national ambitions into lasting results. At the same time, discussions surrounding Red Sea access, Abay River including the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD) and regional security highlighted the complex geopolitical environment in which Ethiopia is pursuing its development priorities. Tana Forum Puts African Leadership and Economic Sovereignty in Focus The 12th Tana High-Level Forum on Security in Africa brought African leaders, policymakers and experts to Bahir Dar to examine pathways to peace amid economic uncertainty, geopolitical competition and shifting global power dynamics. Addressing the forum, Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed emphasized the need for African-led solutions, stronger collective action and economic sovereignty, stressing the importance of enabling the continent to shape its own future rather than remain on the margins of global decision-making. The African Union echoed the call for greater cooperation and strategic independence, underscoring the importance of collective capacity in navigating an increasingly complex international environment. Ghanaian President John Dramani Mahama described the Tana Forum as an authentic African platform for candid reflection and strategic foresight. The gathering provided an opportunity to assess the continent’s security challenges and explore solutions grounded in African realities, priorities and experiences. Prime Minister Abiy’s engagements with Kenya’s Deputy President Kithure Kindiki and Mozambique’s President Daniel Chapo further reinforced the diplomatic dimension of the gathering. His joint visit with President Mahama to Fasilides Castle in Gondar also brought Ethiopia’s historical heritage into the wider program of high-level engagements. Beyond the discussions themselves, the forum raised a fundamental question: how can Africa translate its abundant resources, demographic potential and collective influence into greater economic independence and geopolitical agency? For Ethiopia, the gathering offered an opportunity to contribute to this continental debate while strengthening engagement with African partners. Megech Dam Links Infrastructure with Food and Water Security While the Tana Forum focused on Africa’s strategic future, the inauguration of the Megech Dam in Gondar demonstrated how Ethiopia is pursuing development through investment in critical infrastructure. Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed officially inaugurated the project, which has a storage capacity of 185 million cubic meters and is expected to support irrigation across more than 17,000 hectares of farmland. The dam will also provide drinking water to Gondar and surrounding towns. Its anticipated benefits extend beyond water storage. By supporting irrigation, the project is expected to strengthen agricultural productivity, improve food security and reduce farmers’ dependence on seasonal rainfall. It also offers opportunities for employment, fisheries, tourism and urban agriculture. The project illustrates the relationship between infrastructure investment and broader economic transformation. Reliable water supplies can support agricultural production, expand economic activity and improve livelihoods, particularly when complemented by effective management and access to markets. Prime Minister Abiy highlighted the overcoming of longstanding implementation challenges through the Medemer philosophy and emphasized the importance of further development in Gondar. President Mahama, who attended the inauguration, said the project had inspired renewed efforts to advance Ghana’s long-delayed Pwalugu Irrigation Project. His remarks underscored the potential for African countries to learn from one another’s development experiences and adapt successful approaches to their own circumstances. The Megech Dam thus represents more than an engineering achievement. It reflects the broader challenge of converting natural resources into productive assets that support food security, employment and sustainable economic growth. Indigenous Capacity at the Heart of Economic Transformation Ethiopia’s development agenda also places growing emphasis on indigenous capacity—the ability to design, implement, operate and sustain projects through domestic expertise and institutions. Infrastructure alone cannot guarantee lasting transformation. Its long-term value depends on the availability of skilled professionals, effective institutions, appropriate technologies and productive industries capable of supporting and expanding the investments made. Economic developments during the week reflected this wider ambition. Ethiopia and the United States Treasury reaffirmed their partnership in advancing economic reforms and bilateral engagement, while investment outreach to businesses from the United Arab Emirates highlighted opportunities for longer-term commercial partnerships. Meanwhile, Airbus projected that passenger traffic in Ethiopia could grow sixfold over the next 20 years, pointing to substantial potential for aviation and related services. Realizing that growth will require sustained investment in infrastructure, workforce development and operational capacity. Agriculture also remained central to the country’s development priorities, with continued efforts to strengthen productivity and build a more sustainable agricultural sector. These priorities are mutually reinforcing. Economic reforms can help create conditions for investment, infrastructure can expand productive capacity, and technology and skills can improve efficiency and competitiveness. Ultimately, the impact of these initiatives will be measured by their contribution to employment, domestic industries, household incomes and improved living standards. Strengthening indigenous capacity is therefore essential to ensuring that Ethiopia’s development ambitions are not only achieved but sustained over the long term. Red Sea Access and Regional Geopolitics Remain Strategic Priorities Ethiopia’s development ambitions are closely connected to its geopolitical environment, particularly the Horn of Africa and the Red Sea corridor. Discussions during the week highlighted the strategic importance of maritime access, regional stability and the competition among external powers around one of the world’s significant commercial and security corridors. Ambassador Zerihun Abebe emphasized Ethiopia’s geographic position and historical connections to the Red Sea, framing maritime access as an important issue for the country’s long-term strategic and economic interests. As a landlocked country reliant on maritime routes for international trade, Ethiopia has a direct interest in secure, reliable and economically viable access to global markets. Developments around the Red Sea therefore have implications not only for national security but also for trade, logistics and economic competitiveness. Advisor to the Prime Minister on East African Affairs, Getachew Reda, also underscored Ethiopia’s pivotal geopolitical position. Meanwhile, Professor Al Mariam expressed concern over Eritrea’s policies and their implications for regional stability, while criticizing the Cairo–Asmara relationship. These assessments reflect the perspectives of the respective commentators amid continuing regional tensions. The GERD and Ethiopia’s relations with Egypt also remained part of the wider debate. Egyptian analyst Magdi Khalil argued that attempts to obstruct the dam had been a mistake and advocated strategic relations between the two countries. His position highlights the potential benefits of moving beyond confrontation toward constructive engagement. The GERD is central to Ethiopia’s electricity-generation ambitions, while Nile water security remains a major concern for Egypt. Sustained dialogue, cooperation and mutually beneficial arrangements are important to addressing these concerns and reducing tensions. The broader challenge for the region is to reconcile legitimate national interests with the shared need for peace, secure trade routes and economic cooperation. Pursuing strategic priorities through diplomacy and practical engagement offers a more sustainable basis for regional stability than prolonged confrontation. National Dialogue Seeks a Foundation for Lasting Consensus Alongside development and diplomacy, Ethiopia’s National Dialogue continued to focus on addressing longstanding political, social and governance questions through an inclusive process. Organized around eight pillars, the initiative seeks to create space for dialogue on issues affecting the country’s political arrangements, institutions, social relations and future direction. Its significance lies in the possibility of building a broader foundation for consensus in a country whose stability and development depend, in part, on the ability to manage differences constructively. Moving from deliberation toward consensus is an important step, but the process’s long-term value will depend on the inclusiveness of participation, the credibility of its outcomes and the extent to which areas of agreement can be translated into meaningful action. The week’s discussions among African Supreme Audit Institutions also highlighted the importance of institutional accountability and cooperation. Effective oversight of public resources is critical to ensuring that development commitments deliver tangible benefits and that public institutions maintain public trust. Together, these efforts point to a central requirement for sustainable national progress: institutions must not only deliver services and development but also promote accountability, confidence and constructive engagement. Human Capital and Technology Shape Future Competitiveness Ethiopia’s longer-term development ambitions increasingly depend on its ability to equip its population for a technology-driven global economy. Discussions during the week highlighted artificial intelligence, digital skills and private-sector investment in human-capital development, reflecting the growing importance of technological competence across industries. As digital technologies reshape production, services and employment, investment in skills is becoming an essential component of national competitiveness. However, the benefits of technological advancement depend on more than access to digital tools. Quality education, practical training, research, effective institutions and private-sector participation are equally important. These priorities complement Ethiopia’s infrastructure and economic reform agenda. Roads, dams, transport networks and digital systems create opportunities, but skilled people and capable institutions are needed to operate them efficiently and convert investment into productivity. Building human capital is therefore not a separate development objective; it is a foundation for sustaining economic growth, expanding employment and strengthening Ethiopia’s capacity to compete in an increasingly technology-driven world. Connecting National Transformation with African Ambitions Taken together, this week’s developments reveal a common thread linking Ethiopia’s domestic priorities with its regional and continental engagement. The Tana Forum placed African-led solutions and economic sovereignty at the center of discussions on peace and security. The Megech Dam demonstrated how investment in water infrastructure can advance agriculture and food security. Economic reforms, aviation growth and technological skills highlighted the importance of expanding productive capacity, while the National Dialogue and accountability initiatives underscored the role of institutions in building lasting stability. At the same time, debates over Red Sea access, the GERD and regional security demonstrated that Ethiopia’s development trajectory is inseparable from the geopolitical environment surrounding it. The central challenge is to turn ambition into measurable outcomes: stronger institutions, productive investment, skilled human capital, improved livelihoods and constructive regional partnerships. Ethiopia’s ability to advance these priorities will depend on how effectively it mobilizes domestic capacity, attracts sustainable investment, manages national differences and engages with its neighbors. Ultimately, national development and African leadership are interconnected pursuits. A more productive and institutionally resilient Ethiopia can contribute more effectively to continental cooperation, while a more peaceful, integrated and economically confident Africa can create greater opportunities for Ethiopia’s own transformation. © Ethiopian News Agency 2023 Hidden

Read Mastercard deploys AI, Tokenization to strengthen digital payment security By our staff reporter October 25, 2026 Facebook Twitter Pinterest WhatsApp Global payments technology company Mastercard is deploying artificial intelligence (AI) and tokenization technologies to strengthen security across Ethiopia’s rapidly expanding digital financial ecosystem. As Ethiopia expands digital payments beyond cash-based transactions to include virtual cards, mobile wallets and contactless point-of-sale systems, rising transaction volumes are increasing the need for stronger cybersecurity safeguards. Addressing these vulnerabilities is seen as essential to ensuring that efforts to expand financial inclusion remain resilient against increasingly sophisticated cyber threats. Ethiopia’s digital payment transformation is taking place alongside broader policy and regulatory reforms. The government has pursued measures to reduce reliance on cash and improve interoperability among banks, fintech companies and mobile money operators. However, security concerns have intensified alongside the sector’s growth. The National Bank of Ethiopia (NBE) reported that fraud losses reached 1.3 billion birr in 2024, while attempted cyberattacks targeting government and private organisations increased by 115 per cent in the first half of that year compared with the same period in 2023. Speaking to Capital , Shabir Ahmed, Mastercard’s Senior Vice President and Customer Solutions Center Lead for Africa, said secure payment platforms are essential to sustaining digital adoption in emerging markets. “Every single payment requires absolute trust,” Ahmed said. “At Mastercard, we have made substantial investments in our cyber and fraud mitigation capabilities globally. Today, we harness real-time artificial intelligence to evaluate transactions instantaneously.” He said the company’s systems assess risk factors within milliseconds to determine whether a transaction is legitimate or fraudulent, protecting consumers while enabling seamless commerce. Mastercard’s AI capabilities have continued to evolve. In March 2026, the company unveiled a transaction-specific foundation model, a large tabular model trained on hundreds of millions of anonymised transactions. The model is designed to identify fraudulent activity more accurately than traditional machine-learning systems by detecting complex relationships across large datasets that human analysts might overlook. It also aims to reduce false positives, which can result in legitimate transactions, including high-value purchases, being incorrectly flagged as suspicious. The technology marks a shift from conventional approaches that rely heavily on manually engineered features towards more advanced pattern recognition, helping payment providers respond to increasingly sophisticated fraud schemes. Beyond AI-powered risk assessment, Mastercard is advancing tokenization technology to protect sensitive payment information. Tokenization replaces a cardholder’s actual 16-digit Primary Account Number (PAN) with a digitally generated token that can be used for transactions without exposing the underlying card details. These tokens allow payment credentials to be stored and used across mobile devices, merchant systems and e-commerce platforms while reducing exposure of sensitive account information. If a merchant’s database is compromised, tokenized payment data can provide an additional layer of protection because tokens are generally restricted to specific devices, merchants or transaction contexts. This can reduce the risk of card-not-present fraud and the misuse of stolen payment credentials, although the level of protection depends on how the tokenization system is implemented. The benefits of tokenization have been documented in international markets. Industry discussions citing Visa data indicate that tokenized transactions can reduce e-commerce fraud rates compared with transactions using conventional card numbers. For Ethiopia, where digital payment adoption is expanding alongside concerns about fraud and consumer confidence, stronger payment security could play an important role in encouraging wider use of electronic transactions. The technology also supports Mastercard’s local partnerships, including its collaboration with Dashen Bank and Ethiopian Airlines. Recent co-branded offerings, including ShebaMiles Premium Cards, combine travel-related rewards with international payment capabilities across more than 200 countries and territories. As cross-border payments and digital services become more accessible, ensuring that transactions remain secure will become increasingly important for banks, merchants and payment service providers. Tokenization also underpins several consumer-facing payment services. It enables secure tap-to-pay transactions, supports digital wallets such as Google Pay where the service is available, and helps protect credentials used for recurring payments and international subscriptions. “When I travel today, I no longer rely on a physical card; wherever a contactless point-of-sale terminal is available, I simply tap my mobile phone,” Ahmed told Capital . “Through tokenization, you do not expose the physical card number—you use a secure tokenized identifier. Somalia’s public finance debate must reach local communities October 26, 2026 5 min read BM By - Reporter Benadeta Mwaura Somalia, October 26, 2026 - For a resident waiting for treatment at a health facility, a parent seeking a school place or a community hoping for reliable water, public finance is not an abstract debate about government revenue. It is about whether the services people depend on are available, affordable and adequately funded. That is the challenge at the heart of Somalia’s public finance reforms, as the government seeks to strengthen domestic revenue collection and clarify how resources are shared across different levels of government. In the Somalia Public Finance Review 2026: The Next Stage of Public Finance, the World Bank identifies fiscal federalism- the distribution of financial responsibilities and resources across levels of government- as a key constraint on effective public spending and service delivery. The report states that “FMSs and local governments bear increasing responsibility for frontline services and security, yet operate with limited fiscal resources.” The finding raises an important question: how can local authorities be expected to deliver services when the resources available to them may not match their responsibilities? Speaking during a World Bank briefing ahead of the report’s launch, Stella Ilieva, a World Bank Senior Economist involved in the review, highlighted the consequences of uneven resource allocation for ordinary citizens. “Ultimately, this is about ensuring that a citizen’s access to essential services is not determined primarily by where that citizen lives,” Ilieva said. Her observation points to the practical stakes of Somalia’s fiscal arrangements. Where governments have different revenue-raising capacities and responsibilities are not clearly matched to financing, the ability to plan and deliver services can vary across jurisdictions. The World Bank report says expenditure responsibilities across levels of government remain only partially defined and are not consistently aligned with financing arrangements. It estimates that the Federal Government collects approximately 71% of domestic revenue, while Federal Member States have important frontline service-delivery responsibilities. Somalia has made progress in rebuilding public financial management systems and negotiating agreements on fiscal and governance issues. However, the review argues that stronger cooperation is needed to make the allocation of resources more predictable and equitable. This challenge is becoming more pressing as external assistance declines. The World Bank estimates that external grants could fall from around 5% of gross domestic product to below 1% by 2030. That transition will increase pressure on Somali institutions to mobilise domestic revenue and use available resources more efficiently. The issue is not simply how much money the country collects. It is also how that money moves between levels of government, how spending responsibilities are assigned and whether the institutions expected to provide services have the resources and capacity to do so. Related articles Somalia Releases Man From Ebola Quarantine After Two Negative Tests Somalia’s tax reform debate: Why paying more is not the only option The review identifies existing mechanisms for cooperation, including the Finance Ministers Fiscal Forum and the Intergovernmental Fiscal Federalism Technical Committee. It recommends strengthening the arrangements that guide revenue sharing, expenditure responsibilities and coordination between federal and state authorities. For local governments, however, the practical implications need closer attention. District administrations are often the level of government closest to residents, yet their ability to plan services depends on the resources available to them, the responsibilities assigned to them and the systems they have to manage public money. Independent research published by the Institute of Public Finance Somalia in August 2026 examined public financial management in 15 districts across five Federal Member States. The study reported an average score of 3.47 out of 24 on its public financial management strength index, with no district scoring above eight. The study points to challenges in local financial management and the relationship between assigned responsibilities and available resources. Its findings are separate from the World Bank review, but they add to the case for examining how public finance reforms reach the district level. Improving local services will require more than increasing revenue. It will also require clearer responsibilities, predictable funding, stronger financial controls and better reporting on how public resources are used. For citizens, transparency matters because it helps them understand which institution is responsible for a service, where its funding comes from and how they can seek answers when services fall short. Somalia’s federal and state authorities therefore face a dual task: strengthening cooperation over how resources are shared, while ensuring that local administrations have the capacity and funding arrangements needed to fulfil their responsibilities. The World Bank’s message is that stronger fiscal federalism can help mobilise revenue more effectively, distribute limited resources more predictably and connect financing more clearly to service-delivery responsibilities. Whether those reforms improve everyday life will ultimately depend on implementation, and on whether citizens can see the difference in the services available to them. For the parent seeking a school place, the patient needing treatment or the community waiting for essential infrastructure, the question is simple: who is responsible for funding the service, and how can citizens know that public money is reaching the people who need it? Privacy Policy Terms of Service Search Somalia’s jobs challenge: What Rwanda’s skills-to-work model could teach October 26, 2026 6 min read BM By Benadeta Mwaura - Reporter Somalia, October 26, 2026 - For a young Somali entering the labour market, economic growth means little if there is no job at the end of the journey. That is the difficult reality behind Somalia's public finance debate: the country needs more revenue and better spending, but it also needs an economy capable of turning those reforms into opportunities for the hundreds of thousands of young people seeking livelihoods. The World Bank's Somalia Public Finance Review: The Next Stage of Public Finance estimates that a package of proposed reforms could generate about 54,000 new jobs and 250,000 better and more productive jobs by 2033. But the figures come with an important qualification. “These are simulations, not automatic outcomes,” World Bank Senior Economist Stella Ilieva told journalists during a pre-launch briefing. She explained that the modelling assumes the proposed reforms are implemented and sustained over time. The distinction is important for a country where the demand for work is growing faster than the formal economy's ability to absorb new workers. Ilieva said the World Bank's analysis found that Somalia needs about 100,000 jobs every year simply to maintain its current level of employment, meaning the 54,000 new jobs projected under the reform scenario would not, on their own, close the country's employment gap. The larger opportunity, according to the analysis, is productivity. The projected 250,000 better and more productive jobs represent the possibility of moving workers into higher-value activities as reforms improve the wider economy. “This other 250,000 jobs this is more a result of these reforms, Somalia will be able to move to more high value added jobs,” Ilieva said. That raises a question that extends beyond Somalia's public accounts: what does it take to turn economic reform into jobs that young people can actually access? Across the East African Community, Rwanda provides an example of how skills policy can be connected more deliberately to the labour market. A World Bank-supported Priority Skills for Growth programme in Rwanda trained nearly 24,000 young people and workers between 2017 and 2024. According to the World Bank, 82% of participants were employed or self-employed nine months after training. The programme did not rely solely on classroom training. Employers participated in designing courses, while training was directed towards sectors identified as having growth potential, including energy, transport and logistics and agro-processing. The Rwandan experience is not evidence that Somalia can simply copy another country's model. Rwanda still faces substantial youth employment challenges, with more than one million young people aged 16–30 reported as being outside education, employment or training in 2024. But it offers a potentially useful lesson for Somalia: skills programmes become more valuable when employers help determine what young people are trained to do and when outcomes are measured after graduation. That distinction could become increasingly important as Somalia looks beyond simply creating jobs to creating jobs that raise household incomes and productivity. The broader East African experience also shows why the quality of growth matters. The African Development Bank estimates that East Africa remained one of Africa's fastest-growing regions in 2025, with growth estimated at 6.6%, supported by consumption, investment, agriculture and services. Rwanda, Tanzania, Kenya and Ethiopia were among the stronger performers. Yet the Bank cautions that structural transformation remains limited and that the region continues to face constraints in industrialisation, fiscal space and long-term development finance. The World Bank's September 2026 Tanzania Economic Update says the country's economy expanded by 5.9% in 2025, with services such as finance, trade and transport contributing strongly to growth. But the country still faces a major challenge in converting that growth into formal employment. Related articles Somalia Releases Man From Ebola Quarantine After Two Negative Tests Somalia’s tax reform debate: Why paying more is not the only option The World Bank estimates that Tanzania has about 4 million formal-sector jobs, while roughly 2 million people reach working age every year. In 2023/24, only about 156,000 new formal-sector jobs were created, with 54.9% of those new jobs in the public sector. The lesson for Somalia is therefore not simply to chase a higher GDP growth rate. It is to ask whether growth is creating opportunities in sectors where young people can enter, acquire experience, increase their productivity and eventually build sustainable livelihoods. The World Bank's Somalia review identifies several areas where better public finances could support that transition. The report links fiscal reform to improved investment in education, health, infrastructure and other public services, while also proposing reforms to broaden domestic revenue, improve spending efficiency and strengthen institutions. Ilieva said the World Bank's analysis considered sectors with potential for higher-value employment, including fisheries, construction, agriculture and agribusiness. She noted that another report being prepared by the World Bank would provide a broader assessment of where Somalia's future jobs could come from. That could be particularly important for young Somalis who are unlikely to enter the labour market through conventional government employment. The PFR itself acknowledges that improving public finances is not only about balancing budgets. “The key point is that public finance reform is not only about budgets and accounting,” Ilieva said in presenting the report. She linked stronger public finances to growth, employment, poverty reduction and better opportunities for citizens. For Somalia's young population, that connection will ultimately be tested outside government balance sheets. A young person trained in construction will want to know whether construction companies are hiring. A graduate in agriculture will need access to markets, finance, infrastructure and technology. A young entrepreneur will need customers and a business environment that allows a small enterprise to survive and grow. The government can improve revenue collection and public financial management, but the resulting resources must help create the conditions in which the private sector can expand and absorb workers. Somalia's public finance transition comes at a difficult moment. External grants that have helped support the country's fiscal system are expected to decline substantially, while demands for security, infrastructure, human development and climate resilience remain high. The World Bank therefore argues that Somalia needs to build a stronger domestic revenue base while making every dollar of public spending deliver greater value. For young Somalis, the measure of success may be much simpler. Can the reforms help create a labour market where a young person does not merely find something to do, but can build a productive career, earn a decent income and eventually create work for others? Rwanda's experience suggests that one part of the answer may lie in bringing employers closer to training institutions and measuring whether skills actually translate into work. Somalia's own reform agenda will need to find its own path. But as the country moves towards financing more of its development from domestic resources, the most important return on those reforms may not be another figure in a government budget. It may be a young Somali who can finally turn a skill into a job, and a job into a livelihood. October 26, 2026 6 min read BM By - Reporter Benadeta Mwaura Somalia, October 26, 2026 - For an ordinary Somali citizen, the journey of public money can be difficult to follow. A tax may be collected by one level of government, transferred to another and eventually spent on a service delivered at yet another level. When that happens, a simple question becomes increasingly important: who is responsible for explaining how the money was used? That question sits at the centre of Somalia’s next stage of public finance reforms, as the country seeks to raise more domestic revenue while strengthening the institutions responsible for managing and spending it. The World Bank’s Somalia Public Finance Review 2026 finds that Somalia has made progress in strengthening public financial management, including improvements in payroll controls, fiscal reporting and budget transparency. But it also warns that implementation remains uneven, with different financial management systems operating across agencies and between the Federal Government of Somalia and Federal Member States. For citizens, the issue is not simply whether governments collect enough money. It is whether there is a clear trail from money collected to money allocated, money spent and services delivered . The challenge becomes more complicated under Somalia’s federal system, where different levels of government have different responsibilities for raising revenue and delivering services. During a pre-launch briefing on the report, World Bank Senior Governance Specialist Mahmoud Yassin explained that revenue collection currently happens in parallel rather than through one national system in which revenues are collected and then shared. “Each level of government collects whatever revenue they can collect from the territories that they control,” Yassin said. He added that although legal frameworks exist at both federal and Federal Member State levels, there are overlaps in the taxes being collected, making the relationship between the different levels of government an ongoing intergovernmental policy issue. That creates a governance question beyond taxation: when responsibilities and resources are divided, accountability must also be clearly divided. The Public Finance Review says expenditure responsibilities, revenue assignments, intergovernmental transfers and local government financing remain only partially defined and are often contested in practice. It identifies stronger public financial management capacity and clearer fiscal arrangements as central to improving service delivery. One of the clearest examples raised during the briefing concerns the Banaadir Regional Administration (BRA), whose position within Somalia’s federal architecture is distinct from that of the Federal Member States. World Bank Senior Economist Stella Ilieva said the administration's fiscal reporting presents a particular challenge because its reporting requirements are not yet clearly integrated into the same national framework used by the Federal Member States. “It's a significant amount of money that is collected and spent by an entity without proper financial management rules,” Ilieva said during the briefing, while discussing the reporting challenge. Yassin provided additional context, noting that the BRA participates in intergovernmental platforms and receives substantial intergovernmental transfers. He said the Public Finance Review includes BRA data, including domestic revenue and per-capita calculations, but identified a gap around the publication and consolidation of its fiscal reports. The issue, therefore, is not simply whether information exists inside government. It is whether citizens can see, understand and follow that information. The World Bank briefing noted that Federal Government and Federal Member State fiscal reports are published and that the accounts of the Federal Government and Federal Member States are subject to audit and transparency requirements. The report identifies strengthening audit follow-up and accountability as part of the reforms needed to improve public financial management. Related articles Somalia Releases Man From Ebola Quarantine After Two Negative Tests Somalia’s tax reform debate: Why paying more is not the only option The accountability question matters because public finance is ultimately about more than government accounts. It is about whether a school receives the resources it needs, whether a health facility can function, whether roads are maintained and whether local administrations have the resources to deliver the services expected of them. The Public Finance Review finds that weak coordination between levels of government can result in duplication and service gaps. It also says unclear expenditure responsibilities, unpredictable transfers and uneven public financial management capacity weaken the connection between government spending and outcomes. This is particularly important at the local level, where citizens interact directly with the state. The report notes that local governments are fundamental to a functioning multilevel governance system because this is where many public services are delivered and where citizens interact with government. Yet local administrations remain significantly constrained by limited resources, varying institutional capacity and inconsistent fiscal and administrative data. In practical terms, a citizen may know that government has promised a service but may not know which level of government is responsible for financing it, which institution received the money or where to seek an explanation if the service does not materialise. Somalia is under growing pressure to mobilise more domestic resources as external grants decline. The World Bank says the country must therefore move towards a public finance model increasingly anchored in domestic resources, stronger institutions and greater cooperation between levels of government. But collecting more money without strengthening the systems that track and control it could leave citizens asking the same questions. The report consequently recommends measures including stronger payroll controls, improved procurement, integration of core financial systems and stronger audit follow-up and accountability. This is where accountability becomes an essential part of fiscal reform rather than an issue to be addressed after revenue has been collected. If Somalia succeeds in creating clearer rules over who collects revenue, who receives transfers, who is responsible for spending and who must report on the results, citizens could have a much clearer picture of how public resources translate into public services. For a country rebuilding institutions while managing limited resources, the question is not whether every level of government should operate in exactly the same way. Ilieva stressed that effective federalism does not require every jurisdiction to be identical. What is required, she said, is agreement on the destination, greater clarity over roles and practical mechanisms for sharing resources and coordinating decisions. Somalia's fiscal future will involve different governments performing different functions. But from the perspective of a citizen, the accountability chain should be much simpler: Where did the money come from? Who received it? What was it spent on? Who was responsible for delivering the service? And what happened when the promised result was not achieved? Those questions may sound basic, but answering them consistently could become one of the most important tests of Somalia's next phase of public finance reform. Because ultimately, better public finance is not only about balancing government books. It is about building enough trust for citizens to believe that the resources they contribute, and the resources their governments receive, are being converted into better services and better opportunities. The World Bank's 2026 Public Finance Review highlights the complexities citizens encounter in tracking how tax revenues are collected, allocated, and spent. While progress has been made in public financial management, issues persist, including overlapping tax systems and unclear expenditure responsibilities among the Federal Government and Federal Member States. somalia.content: ZAWYA: Somalia finally joins the Africa free trade agreement — TradingView News Search Products Community Markets Brokers More EN Get started News / Zawya / ZAWYA: Somalia finally joins the Africa free trade agreement ZAWYA: Somalia finally joins the Africa free trade agreement Refinitiv 2 min read By Staff Writer Somalia has officially become the 50th State Party to the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA), completing a series of protocol steps needed to be a part of commercial framework. Mogadishu formally deposited its instrument of ratification at the African Union headquarters in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia on September 4 last month but details of formal membership were confirmed this week. AfCFTA Secretary-General Wamkele Mene told an audience at the official opening of this year’s 26th Common Market for Eastern and Southern Africa (Comesa) Summit in Harare, Zimbabwe that Somalia will now start enjoying full rights in the deal. The move grants Somali businesses and investors preferential access to a continental market of over 1.4 billion consumers.“In terms of implementation of the AfCFTA, your excellences, as we speak today, 54 members of the African Union have signed the agreement establishing the AfCFTA,” said Mene.“50 members of the African Union have ratified it. Somalia is the most recent member of the African Union to ratify the agreement establishing the AfCFTA. We congratulate Somalia for being the 50th state party to the AfCFTA, which further strengthens Comesa's contribution to continental trade.”Somalia’s participation adds further momentum to the collective effort to deepen regional value chains, expand trade and build a more integrated and prosperous Africa. It joined the East African Community at the end of 2024, after also receiving formal nod on debt forgiveness by a various international lenders including the World Bank. Gamal Mohamed Hassan, Somalia’s Minister for Commerce and Industry, submitted the instrument of ratification in September following its approval by Parliament and presidential assent from President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud."Somalia's participation in the AfCFTA will create greater opportunities for local enterprises to access continental markets, attract foreign investment, diversify exports and participate effectively in regional value chains, supporting the country's broader economic development," said Hassan on Thursday. The government viewed the agreement as a platform to accelerate industrialisation, attract investment and drive economic growth, adding that the ministry would work closely with the private sector to maximise opportunities arising from membership. The ministry said its next priorities include aligning Somalia's tariff schedules with AfCFTA commitments, developing the required trade instruments and conducting nationwide outreach to help businesses, exporters, cooperatives and small and medium-sized enterprises prepare for implementation. The AfCFTA Secretariat welcomed Somalia and looks forward to supporting the country as it advances domestic implementation and creates opportunities for the Somali private sector to participate effectively in intra-African trade. Somalia is a member of the East African Community as well as Comesa, both of which are regional blocs that serve as the main anchors for an effective AfCFTA.“Our regional economic communities are the building blocks of the continental market. And in this regard, we value the collaboration with Comesa and other regional economic communities,” said Mene. Among the 21 member states of Comesa, the vast majority have ratified the agreement, including Kenya, Rwanda, Djibouti, Eswatini, Uganda, Egypt, Ethiopia, Zimbabwe, Tunisia, Mauritius, Malawi, Zambia, Burundi, Seychelles, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Comoros, Madagascar and, most recently, Somalia. The 50 ratifying nations include Ghana, Kenya, Rwanda, Niger and Chad in the initial group, followed by a broad coalition across the continent, with Comoros, Mozambique, Liberia, Madagascar and Somalia among the most recent members. The AfCFTA aims to boost intra-African trade by lowering trade barriers and establishing a unified framework for the seamless movement of goods and services across the continent. © Copyright 2026 Nation Media Group. Mogadishu could gain skills and revenue, depending on terms neither side has yet made public. Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Share on Whatsapp Share by printing Copied! Photo by Anadolu Images. O n October 9, at the International Astronautical Congress in Antalya, Industry and Technology Minister Mehmet Fatih Kacır said Türkiye was building a launch site in Somalia for its own rockets and missiles and for the growing world demand for launches. Reports of possible missile testing at the site had surfaced months earlier, but this time a minister was speaking in public. Somalia supplies the land, and much of what the deal means for both countries will be settled long before anything leaves the pad. President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan had confirmed four days earlier that construction was under way, and described it as a contribution to Africa’s space ecosystem. Kacır announced the completion of feasibility and design work in December 2025, and in Antalya he described the site as a very large area allocated to Türkiye. It belongs to Türkiye’s National Space Program , whose aim is to launch vehicles developed in Türkiye, and no date has yet been given for the first launch from Somali soil. Türkiye’s relationship with Somalia grew closer during the 2011 famine and now runs through military training, maritime security and offshore energy exploration. The spaceport takes that cooperation into commercial launches, a business neither country has yet operated. Somalia’s government has welcomed the project. What it has agreed to on land use, commercial revenue and oversight has not been published. Read: Energy Push in Somalia: The Next Phase of Türkiye’s Multi-Layered Strategy A coast close to the equator Warsheikh sits about 2.3 degrees north of the equator. Europe’s spaceport at Kourou, in French Guiana, lies at roughly five degrees. A rocket flying east into a low-inclination orbit picks up speed from the Earth’s rotation and needs less energy to get there, and from Somalia’s eastern shore the flight path heads straight out over the Indian Ocean. Kacır said the feasibility studies had ranked Somalia as the most favorable location, and pointed to cost as well: an equatorial launch, he said, can run about 30 percent cheaper than a comparable one from Türkiye. He also set a target in Antalya. A 400-kilogram Turkish satellite is to reach a 550-kilometer orbit aboard the domestically developed Şimşek-1 by the end of 2027. Whether that mission will fly from Somalia, he did not say. The 2027 target gives the launcher a timetable. The Somali facility has no comparable public deadline. Finding buyers is another matter. African governments have so far purchased launches abroad, from India, China, Europe and the United States. Their combined space budgets rose to $828 million in 2026 from $627 million a year earlier, although much of that money is tied to satellites, observatories and ground infrastructure. A working spaceport on the continent would still give African operators one more option, if its prices and reliability can compete with established providers. Ankara is looking further afield as well. Arif Karabeyoğlu, a board member of the Turkish Space Agency, said at the congress that the spaceport would serve global operators as well as Turkish vehicles. Turning that intention into contracts requires a safety record the facility has yet to build. Read: Why Ankara wants stability from Ethiopia to Somalia From Malindi to Alcântara Somalia would not be the first African state to host a launch site run by a foreign partner. In 1967 Italy began sending satellites into orbit from platforms off the Kenyan coast near Malindi. Nine had gone up by 1988, when the launches stopped, although the ground installations stayed in use. Kenya and Italy renegotiated the arrangement for the Luigi Broglio Space Centre in 2016, and the new agreement took effect in 2020. It provides for an annual land-use payment starting at $250,000, with a $50,000 increase every five years. Kenya is entitled to half the profits from commercial services sold to third parties, has a role in managing the facility and retains authority over launch approvals. Yet in 2023 Kenya’s defense minister, Aden Duale, told a parliamentary committee that Kenyans had yet to see significant tangible benefits. The center, the committee heard, had been reluctant to disclose its commercial activities in full. At Alcântara, in Brazil, the trouble lay on land. Quilombola communities displaced by the space program have contested the area for decades. Brazil signed its 2019 safeguards agreement with Washington while the dispute was still open, and only in September 2024 did a settlement clear the way for land titles. The Inter-American Court of Human Rights ruled on the case two months later, in a judgment covering 171 communities. Some 45,900 hectares were titled in March 2026, although other parts of the settlement remain unfinished. Around Warsheikh, the people who live and fish along the coast will have their own questions about access to land and sea once launches begin. Somalia could earn revenue, train engineers and build technical services around the site. How much of this materializes rests on details still out of public view, among them the length of the lease, the division of earnings and responsibility when something goes wrong. Somali engineers would benefit most from working directly on the facility’s operations, with training tied to jobs they can actually take up. Liability for damage, including harm to fishing grounds, is easier to agree in advance than to dispute after an accident. Residents in Warsheikh will also want to know which parts of the coast are to close on launch days and what procedures will apply in an emergency. Kacır’s mention of missiles stood out in Antalya. He did not say which systems would be tested at the site or under what rules. Mogadishu will want those answers, and so will any foreign company thinking of booking a launch, because a site that hosts both civilian services and missile launches has to decide how safety zones are drawn and who sets the launch calendar. A successful first launch from Warsheikh would be a major achievement for Türkiye. Keeping the site busy afterwards is slower work, and it depends on customers coming back and on rules that both governments can actually enforce. Somalia has made its coast available for a project whose ambitions reach far beyond it. The terms on which it did so deserve to be made public. الدقيقة الثانية من الوقت المحتسب بدلاً من الضائع للشوط الأول، ليمنح الفريق التونسي انتصاراً ثميناً على أرضه، بعد مواجهة اتسمت بأهمية كبيرة للطرفين. وكانت مباراة الذهاب، التي أُقيمت في مدينة لومومباشي الكونغولية الأسبوع الماضي، قد انتهت بالتعادل 1-1، ليحسم الأفريقي التأهل بمجموع المباراتين بنتيجة 2-1. وبهذا الإنجاز، أصبح الأفريقي الممثل الثاني للكرة التونسية في مرحلة المجموعات هذا الموسم، إلى جانب غريمه التقليدي الترجي التونسي، فيما تبخرت آمال مازيمبي في مواصلة مشواره نحو اللقب السادس في تاريخه، والأول منذ عام 2015. ويطمح الأفريقي إلى استعادة أمجاده القارية والمنافسة على لقبه الثاني في البطولة، بعدما سبق له التتويج بدوري أبطال أفريقيا عام 1991. نواذيبو الموريتاني يقلب تأخره ويعبر إلى المرحلة الرئيسية وفي العاصمة الموريتانية نواكشوط، انتزع نواذيبو بطاقة التأهل إلى مرحلة المجموعات، بعدما تغلب على ضيفه سان بيدرو الإيفواري بنتيجة 2-0، على ملعب «شيخ ولد بيديا»، في إياب الدور التمهيدي الثاني. وبدأ الفريق الموريتاني المواجهة بقوة، وافتتح كارتييه ديمبيلي التسجيل في الدقيقة العاشرة، ليمنح أصحاب الأرض تقدماً مبكراً أعاد المواجهة إلى نقطة التعادل في مجموع المباراتين. وفي الدقيقة 53، أضاف شيخ خطاب الهدف الثاني لنواذيبو، ليعزز فرص فريقه في حسم بطاقة التأهل ويمنحه الأفضلية اللازمة بعد خسارة مباراة الذهاب بنتيجة 2-1 خارج أرضه. وبهذا الفوز، عوض نواذيبو خسارته في اللقاء الأول، ليتفوق بنتيجة 3-2 في مجموع المباراتين، ويواصل حضوره في المنافسات القارية، بعدما نجح في استثمار عاملي الأرض والجمهور لحسم المواجهة. ويمثل التأهل خطوة مهمة للنادي الموريتاني، الذي نجح في تجاوز عقبة منافس إيفواري بعد مواجهة امتدت حساباتها إلى المباراتين، ليحجز مكانه بين أندية مرحلة المجموعات. المغرب الفاسي يحسم التأهل بهدف قاتل في أبيدجان بدوره، تأهل المغرب الفاسي إلى مرحلة المجموعات، بعدما حقق فوزاً ثميناً على أسيك ميموزا الإيفواري بنتيجة 2-1 في العاصمة أبيدجان، مستفيداً من تعادله في مباراة الذهاب بنتيجة 1-1 في مكناس. وبعد انتهاء الشوط الأول بالتعادل السلبي، افتتح الكونغولي كريستوفر إيبايي التسجيل للمغرب الفاسي، قبل أن يتمكن كيفين باكارا من إدراك التعادل لأسيك ميموزا، لتزداد صعوبة المواجهة مع اقتراب نهايتها. وبينما كانت المباراة تتجه إلى ركلات الترجيح، خطف خالد بابا هدف الفوز للمغرب الفاسي في الدقيقة السابعة من الوقت المحتسب بدلاً من الضائع، ليمنح فريقه انتصاراً خارج أرضه بنتيجة 2-1 ويحسم تأهله. وجاء الهدف المتأخر ليضع حداً لمواجهة قوية بين الفريقين، ويمنح النادي المغربي بطاقة العبور بمجموع المباراتين بنتيجة 3-2. ولحق المغرب الفاسي بمواطنه نهضة بركان، وصيف البطولة، الذي ضمن بدوره التأهل بعد إقصاء ستار سبورت أكاديمي السيراليوني، بالفوز عليه ذهاباً وإياباً. ويعزز تأهل الفريقين الحضور المغربي في المرحلة المقبلة من البطولة، بعدما نجحا في تجاوز منافسيهما في الدور التمهيدي الثاني. الهلال السوداني يكرر فوزه على سيداما بونا وفي العاصمة الرواندية كيغالي، التي يتخذها الهلال السوداني ملعباً بيتياً، كرر الفريق فوزه على ضيفه سيداما بونا الإثيوبي بنتيجة 2-0، ليحجز مقعده في مرحلة المجموعات. وكان الهلال قد فاز بالنتيجة نفسها في مباراة الذهاب، ليحسم التأهل بمجموع المباراتين بنتيجة 4-0، مؤكداً تفوقه على منافسه في المواجهتين. وجاءت ثنائية الفريق السوداني في الشوط الأول، إذ افتتح إرنست لوزولو التسجيل في الدقيقة 33، قبل أن يضيف محمد عبد الرحمن «الغربال» الهدف الثاني في الوقت المحتسب بدلاً من الضائع للشوط. ومنح الانتصار الهلال فرصة مواصلة مشواره القاري، كما عوض جماهيره جزئياً عن خروج غريمه التقليدي المريخ من المسابقة، بعدما ودع البطولة السبت على يد حوريا الغيني بركلات الترجيح. وبهذا التأهل، يواصل الهلال تمثيل الكرة السودانية في البطولة، وسط تطلعات إلى تقديم أداء قوي في مرحلة المجموعات والمنافسة على بلوغ الأدوار الإقصائية. سيمبا وكولوم يكملان قائمة المتأهلين وشهدت بقية مباريات الدور التمهيدي الثاني تأهل سيمبا التنزاني، بعدما حقق فوزاً عريضاً على فريق 15 أوغوستو القادم من غينيا الاستوائية بنتيجة 3-0. وجاء الانتصار ليمنح سيمبا تفوقاً كبيراً في مجموع المباراتين بنتيجة 9-1، بعدما كان قد حقق نتيجة إيجابية في لقاء الذهاب، ليعبر إلى المرحلة المقبلة بأفضلية واضحة. كما تأهل كولومب الكاميروني إلى مرحلة المجموعات، عقب فوزه على تينغيت السنغالي بهدف دون رد في مباراة الإياب، مستفيداً من انتصاره في لقاء الذهاب بنتيجة 2-0، ليحسم المواجهة بمجموع 3-0. وتعكس هذه النتائج اتساع رقعة المنافسة بين أندية القارة، مع نجاح فرق من تونس وموريتانيا والمغرب والسودان وتنزانيا والكاميرون في حجز مقاعدها بالمرحلة الرئيسية من البطولة. قرعة المجموعات الأربعاء المقبل تتجه أنظار الأندية المتأهلة إلى قرعة مرحلة المجموعات من دوري أبطال أفريقيا، المقرر إجراؤها الأربعاء المقبل، حيث ستتحدد مواجهات المرحلة المقبلة ومسارات المنافسة نحو الأدوار الإقصائية. وتكتسب القرعة أهمية كبيرة بالنسبة إلى الفرق التي تجاوزت الدور التمهيدي، إذ ستتعرف من خلالها على منافسيها في مجموعاتها، في مرحلة تتطلب الاستعداد لمواجهات أكثر صعوبة أمام أندية تسعى بدورها إلى المنافسة على اللقب القاري. ومع اكتمال تأهل مجموعة من الأندية، تتطلع الفرق إلى استثمار نتائجها الإيجابية في الدور التمهيدي ومواصلة المشوار نحو الأدوار المتقدمة، بينما تبدأ الأندية المتأهلة الاستعداد لمرحلة جديدة من المنافسة على أحد أبرز ألقاب كرة القدم الأفريقية.
